Quick presets that set the CPU governor across all clusters at once. Balanced uses schedutil (good all-rounder), Performance locks to the highest frequency, Powersave locks to the lowest.

Decides how fast the CPU ramps up or down in response to load. schedutil tracks workload closely; performance always runs at max; powersave always runs at min; conservative ramps up slowly to save power.
Sets the minimum and maximum clock speed for each CPU cluster (Little/Big/Prime). A higher minimum improves responsiveness; a lower maximum saves battery and reduces heat.
Enables or disables individual CPU cores. Disabling a core can reduce heat and power draw; re-enabling it restores full parallel throughput. Core 0 cannot be disabled.
Tunes the GPU governor, min/max frequency, and power level. Higher frequencies improve graphics smoothness; lower ones save battery. Most noticeable in games and heavy UI rendering.

Applies a thermal profile that controls how aggressively the kernel throttles the CPU and GPU under heat. Conservative profiles protect the hardware; permissive profiles allow sustained peak performance at higher temps.

A compressed RAM disk used as swap. Enabling ZRAM and increasing its size lets the system keep more apps in memory. The compression algorithm (lz4, zstd, etc.) trades CPU overhead for compression ratio.

How eagerly the kernel moves pages from RAM to ZRAM/swap. Lower values (e.g. 10–40) keep more data in RAM for snappier multitasking; higher values (60–100) free RAM sooner at the cost of extra CPU for decompression.

The percentage of RAM that can hold unwritten (dirty) data before the kernel forces a flush to storage. A higher ratio batches more writes for throughput; a lower ratio flushes more often, reducing data-loss risk on sudden power-off.
The threshold at which the kernel quietly starts flushing dirty pages in the background. Must be lower than Dirty Ratio. Tuning this shifts when background I/O begins without blocking the foreground.
How often (in seconds) the kernel wakes up to flush dirty pages to storage. Longer intervals reduce wake-ups and save power; shorter ones keep on-disk state more current.
How long (in centiseconds) a dirty page can stay in memory before it must be written. Lowering this caps the age of unwritten data; raising it defers I/O for better throughput.

The minimum amount of RAM (in KB) the kernel reserves as a free buffer. A higher value gives the kernel more headroom to handle sudden allocations without triggering the OOM killer; too high wastes usable memory.
